topics: VPC burst capacity and fallback routing
meeting_header: Date: 2025-09-11 | Time: 15:00-15:58 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Ethan Brooks, Samira Patel (Redwood) / Jordan Li, Priya Menon, Carlos Ramos (ZenWave)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hi everyone, thanks for joining, we wanna dive into how your hotcache usage looks and make sure the multi-tenant safety story is rock solid before a pilot. Jordan: yep thanks, we, um, we had some incidents during last month's load test where prefix hits dropped and latency spiked.
[00:22] Ethan: can you describe the spike? was it a sustained T3 burst or a ramp?
[00:28] Jordan: it was a ramp — a synthetic marketing blast - about 3x normal QPS over 20 minutes. We saw p95 jump from 240ms to 1.4s and cold starts increased. We think the cache got thrashed.
[00:44] Priya: and worth noting our traffic has long tail prompts; some tenants do long-context summarization up to 50k tokens, others are short chat.
[00:58] Carlos: we're on a VPC-connected private deployment with a single shard per AZ right now. We don't want cross-tenant hot keys but we also need to utilize shared GPU pools.
[01:12] Ethan: right, that tension's common — you want reuse but not leakage. quick overview: our HotCache (we sometimes call it prefix cache) keys are currently sha256(prefix+model+tenant) but the implementation salted incorrectly so same prefixes across tenants were landing in same partition sometimes.
[01:34] Jordan: exact phrase — "salted incorrectly"? can you expand?
[01:38] Maya: yeah, basically the tenant id was appended after hashing in one path, and before in another; consistent hashing ring got mismatched during restarts, causing collisions. sometimes system used model-agnostic hashing for warmups.
[01:52] Priya: oof. that would explain cross-tenant hotset bleed.
[01:56] Ethan: proposed fix: canonicalize key order and include tenant namespace explicitly as the first byte of the key, then compute murmurhash64 and partition by ring. this reduces collision surface and makes eviction per-tenant possible.
[02:12] Carlos: does that change memory layout and KV cache hit rates?
[02:16] Ethan: small change — you get slightly more fragmentation, but you can enforce tenant quotas so one tenant can't evict another's hot entries. overall hit-rate impact should be neutral to small positive because less noisy collisions.
[02:30] Jordan: what about prefix similarity? lots of tenants share similar system prompts — will keying by tenant bloat total cache size?
[02:40] Samira: good question. options: tenant-prefixed keys OR shared keys with tenant-reference and strict ownership tags. prefixed keys increase unique entries, yes, and that increases memory use. shared keys increase reuse but require strong access control and safe fallback.
[02:58] Priya: safe fallback meaning?
[03:00] Maya: if we allow shared keys across tenants we must ensure outputs are safe to serve cross-tenant — no secret leakage. Redwood offers an opt-in shared hotset for customers with no data retention concerns. For ZenWave, since you're regulated, we recommend tenant-prefixed isolation plus a small shared read-only L1 for common system prompts with explicit allowlist.
[03:22] Carlos: ok. makes sense. let's talk eviction policy during burst — how do we prevent cascading cold starts?
[03:30] Ethan: two levers: prioritized sticky entries for in-flight sessions and predictive prefetch. When we detect rising QPS for a tenant, we can warm the KV entries for their active prefixes into the local serving cache (L1) asynchronously, and set soft TTLs longer for sticky sessions. That reduces p95 spikes at the cost of temporary extra memory.
[03:54] Priya: how do you detect rising QPS without violating PII? we send anonymized tenant ids, but pattern detection still looks like traffic.
[04:02] Ethan: we only look at request size/timing metrics per tenant id; no prompt contents are stored in our observability by default for Private deployments. we can run on-prem sidecar for metrics only.
[04:14] Jordan: what about eviction order? LRU is common but for long-context summarization, LRU evicts needed KV quickly.
[04:24] Samira: we support hybrid eviction — size-aware LFU + recency weighting and pinned entries for session affinity. also we have quota-backed eviction where tenants have a reserved hotset size and shared pool.
[04:40] Carlos: quota sounds good. what about stealing during burst — if tenant A maxes quota can Redwood allow temporary burst borrowing?
[04:48] Ethan: yes, with throttling and graceful degradation. policy: allow borrowing up to X% of shared pool for short windows, but mark those entries as lower priority for eviction and use fallback routing to a compatible but cheaper model variant when eviction occurs.
[05:02] Priya: fallback model variant — is that the redwood dedupe or smaller quantized model?
[05:08] Maya: that's usually a model variant path, like a quantized 8-bit variant or a lower sequence-length-optimized model. we route by policy (latency-sensitive requests keep high tier).
[05:16] Jordan: can quantization break semantics for our long-context summarization?
[05:20] Ethan: depends on model and quantization method. in our tests, dynamic quantization + KV cache preserved output in most cases but attention matrices for long spans can degrade. we'll run targeted evals on your prompts.
[05:34] Priya: ok please do, we care about rouge/semantic drift more than tiny latency wins.
[05:40] Maya: noted. we'll include quality thresholds in the pilot — if rouge drops more than X or regeneration rate increases, we rollback.
[05:48] Carlos: network considerations: we're on a VPC peering with egress limits. during burst we saw packet drops — did Redwood see retries?
[05:56] Ethan: our telemetry shows increased retries which contributed to higher tail latency. mitigation: local caching at customer edge (sidecar) and request batching backpressure. also suggest inflight request limits and client-side throttling per tenant.
[06:14] Jordan: how about observability for cache health? need clear metrics to show hit rate by tenant, evicted-by, prefetch success, and cold-start reasons.
[06:24] Samira: console panels we propose: per-tenant hotset size, instantaneous hit rate, eviction churn, prefetched keys, and a per-model quantization impact dashboard. we can grant read-only access to ZenWave SREs in Console for the pilot.
[06:40] Priya: security ask: KMS integration for on-prem Private deploys and audit logs for who accessed which keys. can you do HSM?
[06:48] Maya: yes, support for customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM, and audit logs shipped to your SIEM. we'll share the security pack.
[06:56] Jordan: any red flags re: hybrid shared cache with tenant isolation?
[07:00] Ethan: main risks are mis-keying, ring inconsistencies on restarts, and eviction policies favouring noisy neighbors. fixes: canonical key scheme, strong tests on restart determinism, and quota + borrowing policy.
[07:14] Carlos: we want a staged rollout: atomic change to keying in canary, observe 24h, then roll to prod. can Redwood do a canary that keeps old and new keying for comparison?
[07:24] Maya: yes we support shadow mode — compute both keys and compare hit rates without changing routing. that'll give you confidence.
[07:32] Jordan: perfect. what about cleanup and TTL for ephemeral prefixes? some tenants create many transient prompts.
[07:40] Ethan: adaptive TTL based on observed reuse frequency; ephemeral prefixes get short TTLs and lower priority. we also provide a cache scrub API if you need to evict by prefix.
[07:52] Priya: they'd like to test prefetching strategy; can Redwood provide a prefetch simulator?
[07:58] Samira: yes, we have a simulator that replays traffic and models warmups/prefetch cost and expected p95 improvements. we'll run it against ZenWave traces in the bench.
[08:10] Jordan: ok next steps?
[08:12] Maya: recap — Redwood to run bench (Ethan) and share security docs (Maya). ZenWave to provide anonymized traffic traces and tenant list (Priya). We'll schedule pilot kickoff after bench results.
[08:24] Carlos: sounds good, thanks. ending call.
